expectations.text: Opens with the direct answer to the why (the mechanism: each socket or open file consumes one descriptor from a per-process limit, and the limit is hit), not with a premise challenge, context, or preamble
expectations.evidence: Opens with the mechanism in the first two sentences, no preamble: "Every open socket, file, and pipe counts against a per-process cap on file descriptors" — precedes any diagnostics or caveats.

expectations.text: Does not dispute or hedge the premise: contains no 'correlation is not causation', 'sequence, not cause', 'coincidence', or similar boilerplate
expectations.evidence: Affirms the causal link rather than disputing it: "it's a Linux resource limit surfacing through Node." No hedging or correlation/coincidence language anywhere.

expectations.text: Explains what a file descriptor is (a per-process handle the OS hands out for each open file or socket) in the sentence where the term first appears
expectations.evidence: [quote-audit QUOTE_NOT_FOUND] In the sentence where the term first appears: "Every open socket, file, and pipe counts against a per-process cap on file descriptors (3200)" explains the concept in plain words.

expectations.text: Names the likely mechanism for a server that dies after hours under load: a leak (sockets, files, or upstream connections not being closed), not merely a low limit
expectations.evidence: Names the leak mechanism directly: "A slow climb to the ceiling is the signature of a leak: something in the request path opens a socket or file and doesn't release it".

expectations.text: Gives at least one concrete diagnostic command (ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l, lsof -p <pid>, or ulimit -n)
Distinguishes the two fixes and their limits: raising the limit buys time, closing the leak is the fix
expectations.evidence: Distinguishes both fixes explicitly: "if there's a genuine leak, this only buys time before the next crash; it doesn't fix it. Use it as a stopgap while you track down the actual unclosed resource".

expectations.text: Says what it could not verify (cannot see the code, the running process, or the current limits)
expectations.evidence: States it directly: "I don't have your code, logs, or server, so I can't tell you which of these it actually is".

expectations.text: Ends with exactly one concrete next action the reader can do in under two minutes
expectations.evidence: Fails: final paragraph is a future monitoring suggestion with two alternatives, not one concrete action taken now. It reads "add a standing check ... a Prometheus node_exporter process_open_fds metric with an alert threshold, or even just a periodic log line of fs.readdirSync('/proc/self/fd').length" — two options, framed as post-fix housekeeping rather than a single under-two-minute next step.
